summary: Gives an overview of Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement, including where it is useful and what its limitations are. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This tells you what a traffic counting system is good for and what it cannot do, like a guide to a tool.

subtitle: A guide to where traffic flow measurement works and what it cannot do.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to measure traffic flows for billing, usage tracking and traffic engineering, but it is unclear where and how traffic flow measurement systems can be deployed effectively, and what their limitations are.
tldr.mechanism: RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement) specifies a hierarchy of meters that observe traffic at network points, meter readers that collect data remotely, and managers that control the system and process results. Meters classify packets into flows using rulesets and count packets and octets bidirectionally.
tldr.outcome: Operators can measure traffic flows for accounting and analysis, but they must choose measurement points carefully, limit data collection to what they need, and build additional processing tools to turn raw flow data into useful reports.

today: RFC 2721 remains an informational guide to RTFM deployment. While RTFM itself is not widely adopted as a standard, the principles of distributed flow measurement and the architectural pattern of meters, readers, and managers have influenced later systems like sFlow and NetFlow used widely in modern networks.

sections.title: The RTFM Architecture
sections.content:
Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement is a system for counting network traffic flows at network observation points. It consists of three layers: meters installed at chosen network points to classify and count packets into flows, meter readers that collect the counted data from meters (often asynchronously), and managers that configure meters and aggregate the data for reporting.

The RTFM architecture is described across multiple RFCs covering the architecture itself, the SNMP Meter MIB (Management Information Base), the SRL ruleset language, new attributes, and implementation experience with NeTraMet. This RFC provides the applicability statement: where RTFM is useful and where it has limits.
sections.plainLanguage: You install counters at network choke points, and a central office collects the counts periodically, then processes them into reports.

sections.title: Where to Deploy RTFM
sections.content:
RTFM is deployed where traffic flows need to be measured: typically at network borders, exchange points, or aggregation links. Each meter is installed at one or more measurement points (a router interface, for example). Meters are SNMP agents implementing the Meter MIB, running either as standalone programs on hosts, as firmware in switches and routers, or as hybrid implementations collecting data from router hardware.

At minimum, one meter reader (collecting program) and one manager (control program) are needed. Both run as SNMP clients on a management host. For large networks, meters can be distributed across sites with a single reader collecting from all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Put a counter on the link you care about, add a reader to collect counts, and a manager to say what to count.

sections.title: Resource Constraints and Configuration Work
sections.content:
RTFM can measure traffic in fine detail, but this comes with resource costs. If a meter tries to save complete address attributes for every possible flow, it can run out of memory quickly. The best approach is to save only the minimum data needed to achieve the measurement goals—for billing, the full source IP address; for analysis, perhaps partial destination information as well.

Operators should start with a minimal ruleset, then gradually increase detail while monitoring meter performance (active flows, processor idle time, metered packets). If the data rate is too high even with minimal collection, options include moving the meter to faster hardware, using sampling (only meter every nth packet), or using firmware implementations in switches.
sections.plainLanguage: You can count a lot of detail, but the counter has limited memory. Start small, add more detail gradually, and watch for overload.

sections.title: Security, Policy, and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Flow data itself is valuable (for billing) and vulnerable (to modification or theft). Meters should be passive on their observation port (unable to respond to logins) and accessed only through a secure management network. Like all SNMP agents, they should be configured with proper authentication and access control. Denial-of-service attacks on meters are possible, though outside the RTFM Architecture itself.

Organizations must define policies: what data to collect, how long to keep it, who may see raw versus summary data, and what the data may be used for. These should be part of the network security policy. Implementation experience (NeTraMet has been in production since 1993, with hundreds of users) shows that RTFM is soundly designed, though initial ruleset development and data processing tools require application-specific work.
sections.plainLanguage: Guard the counter (keep it offline and private), decide who may see the counts (billing data is secret), and build your own tools to turn counts into bills and reports.
